# Masked diffusion — MDLM, LLaDA and block generation

Consider a four-token sequence: `The cat sleeps here`. An autoregressive
model generates it by sampling `The`, then `cat` conditioned on `The`,
then `sleeps` conditioned on both preceding tokens. A masked diffusion
model can instead start with four `[MASK]` tokens, reveal `sleeps` first,
then fill other positions using everything already visible on either side.
The output positions exist before their contents are known.

| Reverse-process state | Sequence (positions 1–4) |
|---|---|

# Masked diffusion — MDLM, LLaDA and block generation

An autoregressive model fills the positions of `The cat sleeps here` in
order. A masked diffusion model can fill position 3 first and then use
`sleeps` to help predict the missing tokens before and after it. It starts
with four output positions, all masked.

| Reverse-process state | Sequence (positions 1–4) |
|---|---|

changes.old: not consequences of the name “diffusion”. ## Likelihood, latency and what to compare An autoregressive model assigns an exact tractable likelihood by summing token log-probabilities along the observed prefix. A masked diffusion model defines probability through latent trajectories; its common evaluation uses a variational bound estimated over noise levels and corruptions. Exponentiating a per-token NELBO produces an upper bound on perplexity, subject to estimation error. It must not be relabeled as exact autoregressive perplexity. Loss from one arbitrary mask pattern is not the sequence likelihood either. Predicting a whole block per pass does not automatically make generation faster. An autoregressive decode step processes a new token using cached prefix state; a fully bidirectional denoising step can process the whole sequence again. Report the number of network evaluations, tokens processed per evaluation, block size, cache policy and actual end-to-end latency. Count extra unconditional evaluations if classifier-free guidance is used. MDLM §4.1 describes another form of reuse: when a step reveals no tokens, the next input sequence is identical. A time-independent denoiser can reuse its entire clean-token prediction and apply a new reverse-transition probability without another network call. This is not a prefix KV cache. It becomes invalid when an input token changes, or when a changed time embedding changes the denoiser's input. For an output of $L$ tokens split into $B$ blocks, with $K$ denoising passes per block, the nominal denoiser count is $BK$, not merely $K$.
changes.new:
not consequences of the name “diffusion”. ## Likelihood estimates and generation cost For an autoregressive model, summing the log-probabilities of the observed tokens given their prefixes gives the sequence log-likelihood. A masked diffusion model defines the sequence probability by summing over latent trajectories. The expected NELBO bounds the negative log-likelihood from above; exponentiating its per-token value bounds perplexity from above. A Monte Carlo estimate of that bound still has sampling error. ### Likelihood estimation with a fixed number of masks For conditional likelihood evaluation, [LLaDA §2.4, Eq. (6)](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.09992v3#S2.SS4) estimates the same bound as Eq. (5) by sampling the mask count instead of the noise level. Its predictor needs only the masked response and prompt. For a response of length $L$, first draw the mask count $\ell$ uniformly from 1 to $L$. Then choose exactly $\ell$ positions uniformly without replacement and multiply their summed loss by $L/\ell$. Dividing by $L$ for a per-token result leaves $1/\ell$ times the sum. For the same toy response, take `The [MASK] sleeps [MASK]` with $\ell=2$ and reuse the illustrative target probabilities 0.8 and 0.5. The per-token estimate is $(-\log 0.8-\log 0.5)/2$, about 0.458145. That division is part of the fixed-count scheme. The training example drew a masking probability of 0.25 and then happened to get two masks; its denominator was $L t=1$, giving 0.916291. The two draws look the same, but their mask counts were sampled differently. Neither draw by itself gives a sequence likelihood.
Why averaging over the masking rate gives the same weight Fix a particular mask set of size $\ell>0$. Under Bernoulli corruption its probability at rate $t$ is $t^\ell(1-t)^{L-\ell}$. Multiplying by the per-token weight $1/(Lt)$ and integrating $t$ from 0 to 1 gives $1/(L\ell\binom{L}{\ell})$. If the predictor does not take $t$ as an input, the loss for this mask pattern is the same throughout that integral. The fixed-count sampler gives the pattern probability $1/(L\binom{L}{\ell})$ and uses weight $1/\ell$. The resulting coefficient is identical for each nonempty mask set.
### Denoiser calls and cache reuse An autoregressive decode step can process one new token against a cached prefix. A fully bidirectional denoising step may process the entire sequence again. To compare them, count network evaluations and tokens per evaluation, then measure latency on the same workload. Classifier-free guidance evaluates an unconditional input too, even if the implementation batches it with the conditional input. In [MDLM §4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.07524v2#S4.SS1), if a step leaves every mask in place, the next step receives the same sequence. A time-independent denoiser can reuse its predicted distributions; only the reverse-transition probabilities need updating. A newly revealed token or a different time embedding invalidates that prediction. A prefix KV cache, by contrast, can stay valid while the active block changes. For an output of $L$ tokens split into $B$ blocks, with $K$ denoising passes per block, the nominal denoiser count is $BK$, not merely $K$.
